chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, raising it (to the Prophet), said:

Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The hands are three: The Hand of Allah is the upper one, and the hand of the giver is what follows it, and the hand of the recipient is the lowest of the hands. Therefore, refrain from begging to the extent of your ability. Indeed, sustenance is behind veils; so whoever desires may veil his shame and take his sustenance, and whoever desires may tear down the veil and take his sustenance. And by the One in Whose Hand is my soul, if one of you were to take a rope, then enter the width of this valley, and gather firewood until its two ends do not meet, then he enters the market with it, sells it for a mud of dates, takes a third of it, and gives in charity two thirds of it, it would be better for him than if he were to ask the people, whether they give him or withhold from him.'

key_terms.الَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ: By the One in Whose Hand is my soul

ai.seo_question: What are the three hands mentioned in the hadith regarding begging and sustenance?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* underscores the Shia emphasis on self-sufficiency (*istighna*) and dignity, framing begging as a breach of modesty that obscures one's share of sustenance (*rizq*). The Prophet’s comparison of manual labor to begging highlights the virtue of earning through effort rather than depending on others' charity, a concept deeply rooted in Shia ethical teachings on social responsibility and individual accountability. The mention of 'veils' (*hujub*) suggests that excessive begging may hinder the spiritual reception of divine provision, linking material needs to spiritual states.
